sections.title: EC2, load balancing and Auto Scaling

topics.title: Amazon EC2: virtual servers you rent

kcs.statement: Amazon EC2 provides resizable virtual servers (instances) in an Availability Zone, where you choose the operating system, instance type, storage and network settings. It is AWS's core IaaS compute service.

On-Demand EC2 instances running Linux or Windows are billed per second, with a 60-second minimum. A stopped instance stops incurring compute charges, but its attached storage volumes are still billed.

On EC2 the customer patches the guest operating system and installed software, configures instance firewall rules, protects data and grants the instance permissions through an IAM role. AWS secures the physical hosts, network and hypervisor.

serves.reason: EC2 is the default answer and the main distractor in almost every compute-selection question.

problem_ideas: A startup runs a web app for 3 hours and 20 minutes on one On-Demand Linux instance: how many seconds are billed, and what if it ran only 40 seconds?

topics.title: EC2 instance families: matching the workload

kcs.statement: Each EC2 instance family suits a kind of workload: general purpose (M, T) for balanced web servers, compute optimized (C) for batch processing and gaming servers, memory optimized (R, X) for in-memory databases, storage optimized (I, D) for high local disk I/O, and accelerated computing (P, G) for GPU and machine learning work.

serves.reason: Task Statement 3.3 expects learners to match a workload to an EC2 instance family (for example compute optimized versus storage optimized), and no other topic teaches it.

requires.reason: An instance family is a property of an EC2 instance, so the learner must first know what an instance is.

kcs.statement: An instance type name such as m5.2xlarge encodes the family (m), the generation (5) and the size (2xlarge); moving to a larger size is vertical scaling. T-family burstable instances earn CPU credits while idle and spend them on bursts.

topics.title: AMIs, launch templates and user data

kcs.statement: An AMI is a template containing the operating system and preinstalled software used to launch EC2 instances. AMIs belong to one Region and must be copied to another Region to launch the same image there.

EC2 user data is a script that runs once, as root, at an instance's first boot to install or configure software. A launch template bundles the AMI, instance type and user data so identical instances can be launched repeatedly.

requires.reason: AMIs and user data only make sense as inputs to launching an EC2 instance.

topics.title: Elastic Load Balancing: spreading traffic

kcs.statement: Elastic Load Balancing spreads incoming traffic across targets in multiple Availability Zones behind a single DNS endpoint, so no single server is a single point of failure.
A load balancer runs health checks on its targets and stops sending traffic to any target that fails them until it passes again.

Application Load Balancer routes HTTP/HTTPS (layer 7) by path or host name. Network Load Balancer handles TCP/UDP (layer 4) at very high throughput with static IP addresses. Gateway Load Balancer (layer 3) sends traffic through third-party virtual appliances such as firewalls.

serves.reason: The exam guide asks learners to identify the purposes of load balancers and to pick the right load balancer type.

requires.reason: Load balancer targets are mostly EC2 instances, so the learner must know what an instance is.

topics.title: Auto Scaling groups: elasticity for EC2

kcs.statement: An Auto Scaling group keeps its number of EC2 instances between a set minimum and maximum, starting at a desired capacity, and replaces instances that fail health checks.
Auto Scaling provides elasticity: it adds instances when demand rises and removes them when demand falls, so you pay only for the capacity the load needs.

Target tracking scaling holds a metric such as 50% average CPU. Step scaling reacts to alarm thresholds. Scheduled scaling changes capacity at set times. Predictive scaling forecasts load from history.

serves.reason: The exam guide states that auto scaling provides elasticity, and learners must pick it for variable-demand requirements.

requires.reason: An Auto Scaling group launches and terminates EC2 instances.

topics.title: Containers: an app packed with its dependencies

kcs.statement: A container packages an application with its libraries and dependencies into an image that runs the same way on any host with a container runtime such as Docker.
Containers share the host's operating system kernel, so they start in seconds and pack more densely than virtual machines, each of which runs its own full guest operating system.

topics.title: ECS and EKS: running containers at scale

kcs.statement: A container orchestrator places containers on hosts, restarts failed ones and scales how many run. On AWS the orchestration services are Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS.

Amazon ECS is AWS's own container orchestration service. Amazon EKS runs managed open-source Kubernetes and is the choice when a team already uses Kubernetes or needs portability across clouds and on-premises.
When containers run on EC2 hosts, the customer provisions, patches and scales those instances. ECS itself has no extra charge, while EKS adds an hourly fee per cluster.

serves.reason: Telling ECS from EKS is a standard service-identification item in the compute task statement.

requires.reason: Orchestration schedules containers, so the learner must know what a container is.
The EC2 hosting option and the customer's duties for it build on EC2 instances.

topics.title: Serverless computing with AWS Lambda

kcs.statement: Serverless means AWS provisions, scales, patches and runs the servers: the customer manages only code or configuration, pays for actual use and never manages an instance.

AWS Lambda runs a function in response to an event such as a file upload, an API call or a schedule. It scales automatically with the number of requests, and each invocation can run for at most 15 minutes.
Lambda is billed per request and per GB-second of duration (allocated memory × run time, metered in milliseconds), so a function that is never invoked costs nothing.
Amazon API Gateway is a managed service for creating, publishing and securing REST, HTTP and WebSocket APIs. It is commonly placed in front of Lambda to build a serverless backend.

serves.reason: The exam guide asks learners to recognise when serverless compute such as Lambda is the right choice.

topics.title: Fargate and ECR: serverless containers

kcs.statement: AWS Fargate is a serverless compute engine for ECS and EKS: you set CPU and memory per task or pod, and AWS runs it with no EC2 instances for you to provision or patch.
Choose Fargate over Lambda for containerized services that run continuously or for jobs longer than Lambda's 15-minute limit, when the team still wants no servers to manage.
Amazon ECR is a managed private registry that stores, versions and scans container images. ECS, EKS and Fargate pull images from it at launch.

serves.reason: The exam guide names Fargate as a serverless compute option to choose against Lambda, and ECR is a standard container distractor.

topics.title: AWS Batch and Amazon Lightsail

kcs.statement: AWS Batch runs large numbers of batch jobs, packaged as container images, on managed EC2 (including Spot) or Fargate capacity. Unlike Lambda, it has no 15-minute limit.
Amazon Lightsail bundles virtual servers, storage, databases and networking at a low, predictable monthly price for simple websites and for users with little cloud experience.

topics.title: Choosing a compute service for a requirement

kcs.statement: Pick EC2 when a requirement needs full control of the operating system, runs a specific licensed or legacy application, or moves long-running servers by lift and shift.
Pick Lambda for short, event-triggered code that finishes within 15 minutes, sits idle between events and should cost nothing when unused.
Pick ECS or EKS for containerized microservices: EKS when the requirement names Kubernetes, and Fargate as the hosting option when it says not to manage servers.
Pick Lightsail when a requirement stresses simplicity and a fixed monthly price, and AWS Batch when it describes many queued jobs or batch high-performance computing.

topics.title: Object, block and file storage

kcs.statement: Block storage presents a raw volume to one server, which formats it with a file system. It gives low-latency random reads and writes for operating systems and databases; on AWS this is EBS and instance store.
File storage is a shared hierarchical file system that many servers mount at once over a network protocol such as NFS or SMB; on AWS this is EFS and FSx.
Object storage keeps each file as a whole object, with metadata and a unique key, in a flat namespace accessed over HTTP APIs. Objects are replaced, not edited in place; on AWS this is S3.

serves.reason: Storage-selection questions start from deciding whether the need is object, block or file storage.

topics.title: Amazon EBS: network drives for EC2

kcs.statement: An EBS volume is network-attached block storage that persists independently of the instance. It lives in one Availability Zone and normally attaches to one instance in that same AZ at a time.

An EBS snapshot is a point-in-time, incremental backup of a volume, stored durably by AWS. Snapshots can be copied to other Regions and used to create volumes in any AZ, which is how a volume is moved or restored.

EBS SSD volumes (gp3/gp2 general purpose; io2/io1 Provisioned IOPS for demanding databases) cost more than HDD volumes (st1 throughput optimized; sc1 cold) but perform better. Only SSD types can be boot volumes.

serves.reason: EBS is the block-storage answer the exam expects for EC2 boot and database volumes.

topics.title: Instance store: fast but temporary

kcs.statement: Instance store is block storage physically attached to the EC2 host. Its data survives a reboot but is lost when the instance is stopped or terminated, or when the underlying disk fails.
Instance store gives the highest I/O performance at no extra charge, so it suits buffers, caches, scratch data and data replicated elsewhere; anything that must persist belongs on EBS.

serves.reason: The exam guide lists instance store with EBS among the block storage options learners must tell apart.

requires.reason: Instance store is taught by contrast with persistent EBS volumes.

topics.title: EFS and FSx: shared file systems

kcs.statement: Amazon EFS is a managed NFS file system for Linux that many EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones can mount at once. It grows and shrinks automatically and is billed per GB stored.
EFS lifecycle management moves files that have not been accessed for a chosen period to the lower-cost EFS Infrequent Access storage class.

Amazon FSx provides fully managed third-party file systems: FSx for Windows File Server (SMB, Active Directory integration), FSx for Lustre (high-performance computing and ML), and FSx for NetApp ONTAP and OpenZFS.

serves.reason: The exam guide names EFS and FSx as the file services to identify.

requires.reason: EFS and FSx are introduced as AWS's file storage.

topics.title: Amazon S3: buckets and objects

kcs.statement: S3 stores objects, each up to 50 TB, in buckets. A bucket's name is globally unique, but the bucket itself is created in one Region you choose.
S3 is designed for 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability: standard classes store data redundantly across at least three Availability Zones. It scales to virtually unlimited storage.

Typical S3 uses are backup and archive, static website hosting, data lakes for analytics and media distribution. Versioning keeps earlier versions of each object so overwrites and deletes can be undone.

serves.reason: S3 is the expected answer for object-storage requirements across the exam.

requires.reason: S3 is introduced as AWS's object storage.

topics.title: S3 storage classes: hot to frozen

kcs.statement: S3 Standard suits frequently accessed data. S3 Standard-IA costs less to store but adds a per-GB retrieval fee and a 30-day minimum, for data read about once a month or less. S3 One Zone-IA is cheaper still but keeps data in a single AZ, so it suits re-creatable data.

S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval returns archived data in milliseconds, Glacier Flexible Retrieval in minutes to 12 hours, and Glacier Deep Archive, the cheapest class, within 12–48 hours. Their minimum storage durations are 90, 90 and 180 days.

S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves each object between access tiers automatically based on its access pattern, for a small monthly monitoring fee and no retrieval fees. It is the choice when access patterns are unknown or change over time.

Every S3 storage class trades storage price against retrieval fee, retrieval time and minimum storage duration: the less often data is read and the longer a read can wait, the colder and cheaper the right class.

serves.reason: The exam guide asks learners to recognise the differences between S3 storage classes and pick one for an access pattern.

topics.title: S3 lifecycle policies: automatic tiering

kcs.statement: An S3 lifecycle configuration holds rules, scoped to a bucket, prefix or tag, that move objects to cheaper storage classes after a set age; for example Standard to Standard-IA at 30 days, then to Glacier Deep Archive at 180.
Lifecycle expiration actions delete objects, or old noncurrent versions, after a set age, so logs and temporary data stop adding storage cost automatically.

requires.reason: Transitions move objects between storage classes, so the classes must be known.

topics.title: Storage Gateway: on-premises access to AWS storage

kcs.statement: AWS Storage Gateway is a hybrid cloud storage service that gives on-premises applications access to virtually unlimited AWS storage, keeping frequently used data in a local cache for low-latency access.

S3 File Gateway exposes S3 as NFS/SMB file shares. Volume Gateway presents iSCSI block volumes backed by S3 with EBS snapshots. Tape Gateway replaces physical backup tapes with a virtual tape library stored in S3 and Glacier.
Storage Gateway is for ongoing hybrid access to cloud storage from on-premises applications, not for a one-time bulk transfer of data into AWS.

topics.title: AWS Backup: central backup management

kcs.statement: AWS Backup centrally automates backups across services such as EC2, EBS, EFS, FSx, RDS, DynamoDB and S3, using backup plans that set the schedule and retention.
AWS Backup can copy backups to another Region or to another account in the same organization for disaster recovery and compliance, and Vault Lock can make backups immutable.

topics.title: Choosing a storage service for a requirement

kcs.statement: A boot or database volume for one EC2 instance calls for EBS. Temporary, very fast scratch space that can be lost calls for instance store.
Shared file access from many Linux instances calls for EFS. Windows SMB shares or Lustre high-performance computing call for FSx.

Unlimited storage for files, backups or static web content reachable over HTTP calls for S3. Low-latency on-premises access to cloud storage calls for Storage Gateway. Centrally scheduled backups across services call for AWS Backup.
